$comment: How route geometry survives the wire. Small algorithm, but it explains why responses are not enormous.

meta.title: Encoded Polylines - fitting a route into a string

image_prompt: Create an educational diagram, flat modern style, explaining encoded polylines, as a vertical pipeline of four stages with big arrows between them. STAGE 1 'Raw coordinates': a short list showing 38.50000, -120.20000 then 40.70000, -120.95000 then 43.25200, -126.45300, with a red tag reading 'verbose'. STAGE 2 'Store only the difference': the same points shown as deltas with a caption 'consecutive points on a road are very close together, so the differences are small numbers'. STAGE 3 'Pack into ASCII': a row of 5-bit chunk blocks being assembled into printable characters. STAGE 4 'Result': the single string _p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC_mqNvxq`@ in a monospace box with a green tag reading 'one compact string'. Down the right-hand side, a small map showing the three decoded points joined into a route line, with an arrow from the string to the map labelled 'decoded on the phone and drawn with osmdroid'. Keep all text horizontal and monospace where it is code.

style.look: educational diagram, flat modern, generous whitespace, teaching-poster clarity

spec.problem: A single transit leg's geometry can be a hundred coordinate pairs. Sent as raw JSON numbers that is kilobytes per leg, several times over per itinerary.
spec.idea: Encode the DELTA between consecutive points rather than absolute values, then pack those small integers into printable ASCII characters, 5 bits at a time.
spec.why_deltas_are_small: Consecutive vertices along a road are metres apart, so at 5 decimal places the differences are small integers - and small integers need few bits.

decode_steps.label: Read 5-bit chunks
decode_steps.detail: subtract 63 from each character, take the low 5 bits, and keep going while the continuation bit (0x20) is set

decode_steps.label: Undo zig-zag
decode_steps.detail: the low bit marks the sign, so odd values invert - this is how negatives survive an unsigned packing

decode_steps.label: Accumulate
decode_steps.detail: add each delta onto a running latitude and longitude

verification.note: this is Google's own published reference vector, and it is a unit test in the repo - a decoder that is subtly wrong draws a route that wanders into the wrong part of the city

spec.where_used: OpenTripPlanner returns every leg's geometry this way. transit_client decodes it server-side into [[lat, lon], ...] so the Android app receives the same polyline_latlon shape the driving routes already use, and needs no new drawing code.
annotations: Same format Google Maps uses, so the technique is worth knowing independently of this project.
Precision 5 means roughly one metre of resolution - far finer than a drawn map line needs.
